name: Fire plough
summary: A hardwood stick ploughed up and down a groove in a softwood base — friction with no rotation and no cordage at all.
time: 30-60 minutes to prepare; 1-3 minutes to run

steps.text: Cut a straight groove about 20 cm long and a finger deep into the baseboard, along the grain.
Chisel the tip of the plough stick to a blunt wedge — not a point. A point digs in and stops; a wedge rides and rubs.
Brace the base at a low angle and plough the stick hard up and down the groove, staying in the same track.
Dust collects at the FAR end of the groove and stays there — do not plough through the pile you are building.
steps.why: The Polynesian method builds its ember in a heap at the end of the stroke. Ploughing over it scatters the heat you have accumulated.

steps.text: As smoke thickens, shorten and quicken the strokes without lifting off.
When the heap smokes on its own, tip it into the tinder and blow it up.

verify: A dark dust heap forming at the end of the groove that keeps smoking after you stop.
limits: Very species-dependent — it is a Pacific method built around specific soft woods, and it works poorly with a mismatched pair.
Physically brutal on the arms and shoulders, and it consumes the baseboard fast.
cautions: The stroke drives your hands toward the far end of the board — mind what is in front of it.
Damp wood defeats this even more completely than it defeats the drills.
